title: Underlayment Calculator for Laminate and Vinyl
description: Work out rolls of laminate and vinyl underlayment by area and roll coverage, with waste, worked example, and buying tips.

cover.alt: Illustration of a roll of underlayment on a flooring & tile blueprint background with a measuring tape

keywords: how much underlayment do I need
takeaways: Rolls needed = floor area plus waste, divided by the roll coverage on the label, rounded up to a whole roll.
Common rolls cover 100 sq ft or 200 sq ft, so the same 390 sq ft floor needs 5 small rolls or 3 large rolls with 10 percent waste.
Add 5 to 10 percent for cuts and seams, and never double up underlayment under planks that already have pad attached.
body:
An underlayment calculator does one short job: floor area plus waste, divided by the coverage printed on the roll, rounded up. Most laminate and vinyl rolls cover 100 sq ft or 200 sq ft, so a bedroom and hall job often needs 2 to 5 rolls. Get the count right and you buy once. This guide shows the formula, a full worked example, and the label details that change the answer.

## The formula for underlayment rolls

**Rolls needed = (floor area x (1 + waste percent)) / roll coverage, rounded up to the next whole roll.**

Floor area is length x width for each room, added together. Waste covers cuts at walls, doorways, and the overlap strip many foam rolls use to seal seams. Use 5 percent for one plain rectangle and 10 percent for several rooms, halls, or angled walls.

| Roll type you will see in stores | Coverage per roll | Good fit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Standard foam roll, about 43 in wide x 28 ft long | 100 sq ft | One bedroom or a small job |
| Large foam or combo roll | 200 sq ft | Two or three rooms |
| Jumbo contractor roll | 400 to 630 sq ft | Whole floors and pros |

The 100 sq ft size is the standard shelf roll. Roberts lists its Black Jack foam roll at 100 sq ft per roll, 43 in wide and 28 ft long, and its guide lists other rolls at 360 and 400 sq ft. Home Depot sells a 200 sq ft moisture barrier roll, 120 in wide x 20 ft long, rated for vinyl, laminate, and engineered hardwood. Always read the coverage on the exact roll in your cart, because two rolls that look the same size can cover very different areas.

If your planks have pad already attached to the back, stop and read the flooring box first. Most makers tell you to add no second pad, or only a thin moisture film over concrete. A double pad feels soft for a month, then seams can flex, click joints can break, and the floor warranty can be void. Our [flooring calculator](/blog/flooring-calculator/) counts your planks on the same area, so run both counts together.

## Worked example: a bedroom and a hall

Say you are laying laminate in a bedroom 12 x 20 ft (3.7 x 6.1 m) and a hall 5 x 30 ft (1.5 x 9.1 m). The bedroom is 12 x 20 = 240 sq ft. The hall is 5 x 30 = 150 sq ft. Total floor area is 240 + 150 = 390 sq ft.

Add 10 percent waste for the hall cuts and doorways: 390 x 1.10 = 429 sq ft to cover.

Now divide by roll coverage, two ways:

- With 100 sq ft rolls: 429 / 100 = 4.29 rolls. You cannot buy part of a roll, so round up and buy 5 rolls.
- With 200 sq ft rolls: 429 / 200 = 2.15 rolls. Round up and buy 3 rolls.

Check the result a second way. Five 100 sq ft rolls give 500 sq ft of material, and 500 - 429 = 71 sq ft of spare, enough for mistakes and a future repair. Three 200 sq ft rolls give 600 sq ft, which covers the job with more left over. Pick the 100 sq ft rolls if the price per roll is close, and pick the 200 sq ft rolls if fewer seams matters more to you. Either way, you rounded up like a buyer and you will not run short at the last wall.

## How to measure your floor for underlayment

Measure the full floor, wall to wall, in feet. Do not subtract closets you plan to floor. Do subtract areas with tile or carpet that stay in place.

Break odd rooms into rectangles, multiply length x width for each part, and add the parts. Write the numbers on a rough sketch. Our [square footage calculator](/blog/square-footage-calculator/) handles L-shapes, circles, and triangles if your room is not a plain box.

Measure the longest wall too. Roll width matters in narrow halls. A roll about 43 in (3.6 ft) wide covers a 5 ft hall in two strips with a seam, while a wide 10 ft barrier roll can cover a small room in one piece with fewer seams.

## Pick the right underlayment for the floor above it

Foam rolls in the 2 to 3 mm range are the standard pick for laminate. They soften small subfloor flaws, cut sound, and cost the least. Cork and felt products cost more, feel firmer, and earn better sound ratings for condos that set minimum IIC and STC scores. Very thick, soft pad is a poor match for thin click-lock vinyl, because the planks flex at the joints and can snap on a busy hall.

Over concrete, moisture control comes first. Use a combo roll with a built-in vapor barrier, or lay a 6 mil plastic film first, then the pad. Home Depot lists its 200 sq ft barrier at 6 mil thick with a 3 in overlap for that job. Over a wood subfloor above a dry basement, plain foam is fine in most homes. Compare your floor choice in our [laminate vs vinyl plank cost guide](/blog/laminate-vs-vinyl-plank-cost/) if you have not bought the planks yet.

Roll the pad out as the label directs, butt the seams edge to edge, and tape them. Do not overlap foam seams. An overlapped seam makes a soft ridge that can show through the floor and squeak later.

## Common mistakes that waste rolls

The first mistake is buying by room count instead of area. Two small bedrooms can use fewer rolls than one long living room with a hall. The second is forgetting waste on a cut-heavy job. Our [flooring waste factor guide](/blog/flooring-waste-factor/) explains why 10 percent is normal once doorways and closets enter the plan.

The third mistake is doubling up. Pad on the plank plus a thick roll below feels plush in the store and causes joint trouble at home. The fourth is laying underlayment over a rough subfloor and hoping it hides the problem. Foam hides flaws under about 1/8 in at best. Fill low spots, sand high spots, and screw down squeaks first, while the floor is bare.

## Frequently asked questions

### How many rolls of underlayment do I need for 500 sq ft?
With 10 percent waste you need to cover 550 sq ft. That is 550 / 100 = 5.5, rounded up to 6 rolls of 100 sq ft, or 550 / 200 = 2.75, rounded up to 3 rolls of 200 sq ft. Buy the size your store stocks in the product you picked.

### Do I need underlayment under vinyl plank with pad attached?
No extra pad in most cases. Most makers allow only a thin moisture film over concrete, and some allow nothing at all. Read the box and the warranty sheet. Adding a thick roll under pad-backed planks can void coverage and damage the click joints.

### How much waste should I add for underlayment?
Add 5 percent for one plain rectangular room and 10 percent for halls, closets, and angled walls. Underlayment waste is lower than plank waste because strips can be taped together and reused in closets. Round the final roll count up, never down.

### Can I use the same underlayment for laminate and vinyl?
Often yes for foam and film products, and Home Depot lists its 200 sq ft barrier for vinyl, laminate, and engineered hardwood. Thin vinyl still needs a firmer, thinner pad than laminate in many product lines. Match the pad thickness to the plank maker's limit, not to what feels softest in the aisle.

### Which way should underlayment seams run?
Run rolls across the room so seams do not line up with long plank seams, butt the edges tight, and tape every seam. A taped, flat seam will not move under the finished floor.
